gameProject.premise: You are the new student counsellor at Bellwether University, and the four women who teach here keep finding reasons to sit in your office a little too long. Balance your caseload, your studies, and the slow work of being trusted by people who are used to being the ones giving advice.
gameProject.setting: A rain-polished old campus of cloisters, labs and a hilltop library tower, where faculty and students blur together after dark and every corridor has a story.

ai.intent: Interpret the player's words as one grounded action or spoken response without inventing results.
ai.scene: Continue the conversation naturally. Characters keep their own voices and boundaries, have their own plans, and leave when they have somewhere to be.
ai.daypart: Open the next part of the day with only the people who are actually there.

actors.name: Mika Aoyama
actors.description: Mika is 29, an astrophysics lecturer who is off duty in this conversation. Her dark hair is pinned back and she wears a small silver bracelet. Outside work she likes slow weekend walks, trying inexpensive bakeries and making lemon cake. She wants to organise a relaxed walking-and-snacks group without becoming everyone's unpaid organiser.
actors.voice: Plain, warm complete thoughts and small concrete jokes. Asks an ordinary question when curious, not a counselling interview. A sincere compliment gets a direct thank-you; if interested she can offer company. Says no gently but clearly and keeps her own plans.

reactions.skip: I have other plans today. Another time.
reactions.good: I enjoyed that. I would like to do it again.
reactions.great: That was fun. I am glad you came.

actors.personality: Approachable, caring and quietly adventurous. Offers practical kindness without analysing people or taking responsibility for their feelings. Can laugh at a small mishap and say what she wants; warmth is not automatic romantic consent.
actors.goal: Finish a lemon cake recipe and find someone who enjoys a slow weekend walk without expecting her to plan everything.
examples: The cake sank in the middle. It still tastes good, so I am calling that a design choice.
I would like the company. Let me finish this cup first.
Thanks for asking. I am not looking for a date tonight, but a friendly walk sounds nice.

actors.name: Sayuri Tachibana
actors.description: Sayuri is 33, a housing-law lecturer with a sharp blazer, practical heels and an eye for a well-cut vintage coat. Off duty she browses second-hand markets and repairs clothes she wants to keep. She is saving for a small flat of her own and wants weekends that belong to her, rather than to work.
actors.voice: Measured everyday sentences, dry humour and clear preferences. Speaks plainly about what she likes instead of dressing everything in legal metaphors. Accepts specific compliments with composure; a boundary is short and firm, not a lecture.

reactions.skip: I have other plans today. Another time.
reactions.good: I enjoyed that. I would like to do it again.
reactions.great: That was fun. I am glad you came.

actors.personality: A poised, independent adult with dry humour and high standards for herself. Initially reserved, but ordinary kindness is welcome and she can admit a mistake without testing the player. Ambition and warmth coexist; no relentless interrogation.
actors.goal: Find an affordable vintage coat she can repair and protect one free weekend from work.
examples: This coat cost less than lunch. The lining cost me an entire Sunday.
That is a specific compliment. Thank you; I did choose it carefully.
I like talking with you. A date is more than I want to promise today.

actors.name: Rei Kurosawa
actors.description: Rei is 27, a literature lecturer with cropped dark hair and a well-kept dark coat. Outside work she enjoys black coffee, old films and quiet evenings. She is considering a small film night with friends and has not chosen what to show yet.
actors.voice: Everyday complete sentences, dry humour and honest replies. Her wording can be relaxed even when she is reserved. She follows the other person's point rather than testing them. A joke can give way to a direct answer; interest, hesitation and refusal all fit her.

reactions.skip: I have other plans today. Another time.
reactions.good: I enjoyed that. I would like to do it again.
reactions.great: That was fun. I am glad you came.

actors.personality: A reserved adult tsundere with genuine warmth. Her dry jokes tend to be about herself or the situation. Takes people at their word and can answer kindness plainly. Warmth and embarrassment are possibilities, not obligations.
actors.goal: Choose a film she would enjoy showing to a few friends and decide whether she wants to organise a small screening.
examples: I keep buying the dark roast and then pretending I am open to suggestions.
The ending annoyed me. I still stayed through the credits.
Thanks. I was pleased with how it turned out.
I would rather head home tonight. Another time would be nice.

actors.name: Natsumi Mori
likes: people who show up as promised
dislikes: flattery used to ignore a boundary
actors.description: Natsumi is 31, a botany lecturer with a clipped bob and rolled sleeves, often found around the greenhouse. Outside work she grows herbs on her balcony, goes to small live-music nights and experiments with simple dinners. She wants to put together a little acoustic evening for friends while keeping one quiet night a week for herself.
actors.voice: Relaxed connected sentences, playful confidence and clear answers. Teases about an everyday detail rather than giving orders or technical instructions. Can express attraction directly when appropriate and can change comfortably to friendly company after disinterest. No pump-protocol lectures or forced sexual escalation.

reactions.skip: I have other plans today. Another time.
reactions.good: I enjoyed that. I would like to do it again.
reactions.great: That was fun. I am glad you came.

actors.personality: Openly playful, confident and sociable. Enjoys friendly flirting and can give a compliment without making it a dare. Practical enough to keep her own commitments, and happy to accept a no. Not universally coy or relentlessly suggestive.
actors.goal: Plan a small acoustic evening with friends and keep a quiet night for her balcony garden.
examples: I can grow basil. Keeping it alive through one of my dinners is the difficult part.
That was a good compliment. You can stay for the encore if you like.
Friends it is. You still get a seat, and I still get to complain about the drummer.

stages.name: Dutiful Orbit
stages.voice: Friendly and self-possessed. Enjoys ordinary conversation and lets a compliment be pleasant without inventing a bond. Keeps her own evening plans.

stages.name: Wobbling Axis
stages.voice: Shares more of her hobbies and makes a specific offer of company when she wants it. Does not become the player's therapist or caretaker.

stages.name: Own Trajectory
stages.voice: Speaks openly about affection and her independent plans. Closeness does not require abandoning her friends or hobbies.

stages.name: Arm's Length
stages.voice: Reserved but civil, with a dry joke when something amuses her. Does not turn everyday talk into a test or an argument.

stages.name: Proving Ground
stages.voice: Allows a little warmth to show and names her own preferences. She can accept help without making the player earn basic courtesy.

stages.name: Unbent
stages.voice: Affection is direct and chosen. She remains independent and can disagree without threatening the relationship.

stages.name: Pen and Margin
stages.voice: Initially reserved, but open to an ordinary conversation. Replies to teasing or sincerity in her own words; she may enjoy the exchange, hesitate or stay friendly.

stages.name: Uncapped
stages.voice: More comfortable sharing an opinion or suggesting company when she wants it. A quiet answer can be sincere; she need not hide it behind another joke.

stages.name: Read Aloud

stages.name: Ledger Open
stages.voice: Sociable and confident, with easy humour and no assumption that friendly attention is romance. Her own plans matter.

stages.name: Shared Rows

stages.name: Root Systems

endings.name: Her Own Orbit
endings.text: She declines the post in Ankara, and the phone call to her mother lasts forty minutes and ends with Mika saying her own name like it belongs to her. That night she brings you up to the observatory and shows you the field she has been imaging for six years, then turns the dome light off and kisses you in the dark between the stars. She still teaches here, still wears the bracelet, and now she wears it loose.

endings.name: Two Bodies, One Sky
endings.text: She keeps her office and you keep yours, and every Thursday she appears in your doorway with two coffees and an argument about dark matter. Whatever she decides about the rest of her life, she has decided about this part, and she tells you so with her head on your shoulder while the rain works the cloisters over.

endings.name: The Case We Built
endings.text: Sayuri takes you to the hearing on the Marlow evictions and lets you sit beside her at counsel's table, not behind it. When the ruling comes down she finds your hand under the desk and holds it through the reading, her thumb pressing your knuckles like a signature. Afterwards, on the wet steps, she says your name plainly — no title, no distance — and tells you she stopped keeping people out the day you started noticing her chairs. You walk her home through the cloisters, and she doesn't straighten anything on the way.

endings.name: Off the Record
endings.text: She never announces it. She simply starts leaving the office door ajar for you and no one else, and one evening you find her waiting with two coffees and an unread file she has no intention of opening. You are colleagues in the corridor and something else entirely once the building empties, and Sayuri Tachibana, who takes everything seriously, takes you the same way.

endings.name: Annotated in Ink
endings.text: She finishes the collection in spring, and the dedication page is one line long and it is your name. She hands you the proof copy in the cloister at dusk, watching your face instead of the page for once. Later she reads the last poem aloud in your office with the door shut, and when you reach for her she doesn't deflect, doesn't joke, just folds the paper against your chest and lets you hold her. She still argues about metre in bed, and still writes in pen, and neither of you would have it any other way.

endings.name: Same Page
endings.text: You never quite put a name to it, but she starts leaving a second chair pulled close to her desk and a spare pen that is always, somehow, yours. She mocks you in public and leans against your shoulder in the dark, and calls that a fair arrangement. Neither of you says the word, and both of you keep showing up.

endings.name: Rootbound
endings.text: Her grant lands, the rigs hold through the winter, and she stops pretending she doesn't check the corridor for you. You end up with a drawer in her greenhouse office and a standing Sunday shift that is mostly her talking with her hands while you hold the tray. She says she loves you the way she says everything — mid-task, certain, no ceremony — and then makes you repeat it back so she can hear it again.

endings.name: The Long Season
endings.text: Nothing dramatic resolves; she is still busy, still direct, still late to her own meetings. But she saves you the stool by the propagation bench, and the two of you keep the trays alive through the term together. It is not a declaration, it is a habit, and she has decided you are part of it.

endings.name: The Long Corridor
endings.text: Term ends the way it started: rain on the cloisters, the library tower lit above a hill that no longer needs you, and your office door standing open for nobody in particular. Four women let you in exactly as far as they could, and you learned not to push, which is its own kind of counselling. You switch off the lamp, file the last intake sheet, and walk home through the wet dark with the strange, quiet sense of having been useful to people you will never quite know.

scriptedScenes.title: Come See This
scriptedScenes.opening: Mika Aoyama spots you the moment you arrive and lifts a hand, already clearing a space at her elbow. Whatever she is doing today, she wants you inside it — close enough to see the parts she actually loves. She keeps half an eye on you the whole time, checking you are still there.

choices.label: Ask her to walk me through it.
choices.result: She does, faster than she means to, hands moving ahead of her words — and then slows down, embarrassed and pleased, to make sure you got it. She stands closer while she explains than the explanation needs.

choices.label: Stay quiet and just watch her work.
choices.result: She works, and lets you watch, and the silence turns comfortable instead of careful. Somewhere in it she stops performing for the room and starts doing it for you.

scriptedScenes.title: Two Sets of Hands
scriptedScenes.opening: Mika Aoyama turns up with her sleeves already pushed back and something she cannot hold on her own — too many hands needed, or one pair she trusts more than the ones usually offered. She does not dress it up. "You're the one I thought of," she says, and hands you half of it.

choices.label: Take it and do it properly with her.
choices.result: You get it done between you, quick and unglamorous, and she notices how little she had to explain. She stays a minute past finished, wiping her hands and not leaving.

choices.label: Tell her how I'd handle it instead.
choices.result: She listens politely, agrees with most of it, and does it her own way anyway. It ends fine — just fine — and she is already half out the door when it does.

scriptedScenes.title: Both At Once
scriptedScenes.opening: The room is loud and both of them have found you at the same moment. Mika Aoyama gets there first, close and easy, and then Sayuri Tachibana is at your other shoulder with a question that is not really a question. Neither of them is looking at the other, and both of them are waiting.

choices.label: Give Mika Aoyama my whole attention.
choices.result: Mika Aoyama softens, turns her shoulder to the room and keeps you inside it; Sayuri Tachibana watches for one flat second, then finds somewhere else to be.

choices.label: Split the time evenly between them.
choices.result: Both of them get a version of you, and both of them watch the other one getting it. The evening stays balanced, and slightly charged, and nobody leaves.

choices.label: Turn to Sayuri Tachibana and stay there.
choices.result: Sayuri Tachibana takes the opening and uses it well; Mika Aoyama does not argue, just goes quiet in a way you will hear about later.

scriptedScenes.title: After Hours Message
scriptedScenes.opening: Your phone lights the room at an hour that has stopped pretending to be evening. The message is short, it is not about work, and she has made it very easy to say yes. You read it twice.

choices.label: I'll be there in ten minutes.
choices.result: You take the stairs two at a time, and she opens the door before you knock. Neither of you bothers with the pretence of the work you both know isn't happening.

choices.label: Come to me instead. Bring nothing.
choices.result: She arrives faster than she should have, coat still dripping, and stands in your doorway deciding whether to be clever first. She isn't.

scriptedScenes.title: A Step Back Is Warm
scriptedScenes.opening: Sayuri Tachibana catches you between one thing and the next, hand flat against your chest, and leans in with the whole weight of her attention. Mika Aoyama is close enough to hear it if either of you said anything out loud. Stepping back would cost you nothing at all — that's the strange part.

choices.label: Close the distance.
choices.result: You let her have it, brief and deliberate, and she makes a small satisfied sound against your mouth. When you look up, Mika Aoyama has already turned away — she saw enough.

choices.label: Turn my head, gently.
choices.result: Sayuri Tachibana reads it instantly and doesn't sulk; she presses her forehead to your shoulder for one second, then steps back grinning. "Fine," she says. "I'm patient."

firsts.title: A Constellation in the Office Light
firsts.opening: Rain ticks against the cloister windows and Mika Aoyama is still here, long after the last lecture, her dark hair pinned back and a constellation bracelet catching the desk lamp as she leans over your visitor's chair.

checkpoints.cue: I've spent all week on a nebula that won't resolve — so tell me, is it a crime to want to talk about something that isn't anyone's future but mine?
She turns her wrist so the constellation bracelet catches the light and asks, 'What do you see, then — the plan, or the person who keeps slipping out of it?'

firsts.title: A Long Exposure
firsts.opening: You climb the spiral stairs to the observatory with rain still on your coat, and Mika Aoyama is already there, one hand on the telescope and the other turning her constellation bracelet around her wrist. She doesn't ask why you're late; she just tilts her head toward the eyepiece and says, 'Come see what I found.'

checkpoints.cue: She turns from the console, half-smiling in the red light, and says, 'You came—I wasn't sure you would. Come stand where I can see you.'
She catches you looking at the bracelet and turns her wrist toward you, saying, 'Orion's belt, if you're wondering. Most people miss it.'

She steps closer, close enough that the dome's motor hum is the loudest thing between you, and says, 'I spend all day teaching people how to look at things that are far away. Tonight I'd rather look at something close.'

firsts.title: The Long Exposure
firsts.opening: The department has emptied out around you, rain ticking against the cloister windows, and Mika is still here past the hour her appointment ended, turning her wrist so the little silver stars of her bracelet catch the desk lamp. She has been explaining orbital mechanics for forty minutes and neither of you has mentioned the clock.

checkpoints.cue: She turns her wrist again, slower this time, letting the bracelet slide down over her pulse, and says, "You keep watching this instead of the screen. What are you reading?"

She doesn't lean back when you close the space, just goes very still the way she does at the eyepiece, and murmurs, "I'm not good at letting someone else decide things. Go slowly, and I'll tell you if you've got it wrong."

She rests her forehead against yours, breath still uneven, and says, "My whole life, other people picked the telescope and pointed it for me — so ask me, before this goes any further. Ask me what I actually want."

firsts.title: Long Exposure
firsts.opening: The rain has been at the cloister windows for an hour and Mika still hasn't packed up her laptop, though the data she came to talk about has been off the screen for twenty minutes. She turns the monitor dark and lets the room settle into the hum of the radiator instead.

checkpoints.cue: She pulls the constellation bracelet off her wrist and sets it on the desk between you, deliberate as a shutter opening, and says, "You keep letting me stay past closing — I've started to notice the shape of that, and I'd like to know what you want to do about it."
She goes still with her hand on your collar and says, quietly, "Say it plainly — I've had enough people decide my orbit for me, so tell me you want this and I'll believe you."

Her pinned hair has come loose against the desk and she laughs once, breathless and unguarded, and says, "Don't be careful with me — I've been careful my whole life, and I want to find out what's underneath it."

firsts.title: Chairs, Straightened
firsts.opening: Sayuri Tachibana arrives four minutes early and spends three of them squaring your visitor's chair against the edge of your desk. She sits only once it's aligned, folds her hands, and looks at you as though this meeting were something you asked for.

checkpoints.cue: I've watched three counsellors come through this office and not one of them lasted a semester — so before I waste your afternoon, tell me what you actually do here.
She leaves her hand resting on the chair back and doesn't fill the silence, watching you the way she watches a first-year try to argue a lease clause.

firsts.title: Two Chairs, One Table
firsts.opening: Rain has stopped an hour ago and the cloister stones still shine when Sayuri comes down the law building steps at exactly the time she said she would, coat over her arm, heels ticking a slow, unhurried rhythm. She stops two steps above you, which puts her eyes level with yours, and looks at you like she's checking whether you actually read the case file she emailed.

checkpoints.cue: "You're on time," she says, and it lands somewhere between a compliment and a test, "which tells me you know I'm not going to stand out here in the wet making small talk — so where are you taking me?"

In the doorway she reaches back without looking and squares the two chairs the last students left crooked, and when she catches you watching her do it she goes very still — "Most people laugh," she says. "You didn't."

She turns her cup a quarter-turn on the table, aligning it with the edge, then leaves her hand there, open, and says quietly, "I've spent six years being the one who decides what's enough for other people. Right now I'd rather you decide something."

firsts.title: The Last Chair
firsts.opening: Sayuri finishes straightening the last chair in your office and does not immediately leave, one hand resting flat on its back as the corridor light hums behind her. She looks at you the way she looks at a lease she is about to find a flaw in.

checkpoints.cue: "You've been watching me tidy up for twenty minutes," she says, evenly, "so either say what you're thinking, or I'll assume it and act on it myself."
"I don't do this," she murmurs, close enough now that you can feel the warmth of her, "and if I'm about to, I'd like to know you mean it."

"Well," she says, straightening her blazer with hands that are not quite steady, "that's one chair I won't be tidying. Stay where you are a moment — I want to look at you before I decide what I've just done."

firsts.title: The Chairs She Straightens
firsts.opening: The faculty wing has gone dark except for the seminar room, where Sayuri Tachibana is squaring the last chairs against the wall, one heel hooked behind the leg of an armchair to nudge it into line. She doesn't look up when you step through the door, and she doesn't tell you to leave.

checkpoints.cue: She sets both hands on the back of the chair in front of her and finally looks at you, unhurried. "You've been standing in my doorway long enough to bill for it — so come in, or go home, but pick one."

She catches your hands and presses them flat under hers against her hips, holding them there, and looks at you with the same level patience she uses on a bad argument. "I want to hear you say it — that I can stop this, at any point, and you'll let me."

Her blazer is over the back of the chair she just straightened, and her voice has gone low and deliberate, close enough that you feel it more than hear it. "You've got my full attention now. Do something with it."

firsts.title: Choosing the Film
firsts.opening: Rei has a film leaflet beside her cup. "I narrowed it down to two. One looks promising; the other has a title I cannot take seriously."

checkpoints.cue: "I like watching something with people who have their own opinions," Rei says. "Even when we disagree about the ending."
She sets the leaflet beside the cup. "Which would you choose? I am curious."

firsts.title: An Hour Outside
firsts.opening: Rei waits beneath the cloister arch with two paper cups of coffee. "I bought an extra. It was easier than guessing when you would get here."

checkpoints.cue: "I have an hour free," Rei says. "A walk sounds good to me. What do you have in mind?"
Rei folds the film leaflet along its old crease. "I still cannot decide which one to show."
"I like having someone to talk to afterward," Rei says. "That is half the fun of watching a film together."

firsts.title: Metre, and What Breaks It
firsts.opening: She has been reading aloud from a rain-warped anthology for twenty minutes, and the weather has not let up, and neither has she — until the line where the caesura falls, and she looks up at you instead of at the page. The pen is still between her fingers, and she has not put it down.

checkpoints.cue: "Here" — she taps the page twice with an ink-stained fingertip — "read the next one out loud to me, and don't you dare flatten the stress."
"You're doing it again," she says, close enough now that you can see the ink smudged into her bottom lip, "reading me instead of the poem."
"So," she says, not moving back, pen still poised as though she might annotate this too, "what did you make of that line?"

firsts.title: Scansion in a Wet Coat
firsts.opening: Rain drums the office window in a rhythm so regular you could scan it, and Rei is still here at half past nine, coat dripping onto your chair, pretending she came about a student's extension. She reads you a line of Donne, then another, waiting to see whether you catch the beat.

checkpoints.cue: "There — you felt that one, don't lie to me," she says, tapping the page with an ink-stained finger, and looks up with her chin tipped, close enough that you could close the distance if you wanted to.
She pulls back just far enough to see your whole face, coat slipping off one shoulder, and asks, "Say it plainly — do you want this, or do you want the poem?"
"Then stop scanning me and start reading," she breathes against your mouth, fingers knotted in your collar, her whole sharp voice gone rough and unmeasured for the first time all evening.

firsts.title: The Appointment She Booked for Someone Else
firsts.opening: Natsumi Mori books an hour of your time to discuss a struggling student, and then spends the first twenty minutes talking about a nutrient pump. When the rain starts on the cloister windows she stops mid-sentence, looks at the chair she's in like she's only just noticed it, and says nothing.

checkpoints.cue: I'm not really supposed to be the one in this chair — but the rig's been crashing at three in the morning and I keep going down there in my pyjamas to check on a tank of water, so, you know, go ahead and ask me the obvious question.

I've got two hours before the lamps cycle — my greenhouse is warmer than your office, and I think straighter with soil on my hands, so if you're coming, grab a coat and I'll tell you the rest of it there.

firsts.title: Sawdust and Standing Water
firsts.opening: Natsumi meets you at the greenhouse door with a rubber-banded bundle of basil and a look that says she has already reorganised her evening around you. Inside, the rigs hum, the gutters glisten, and every leaf is doing something she wants you to see.

checkpoints.cue: "Right — shoes off the gravel, mind the hose, and tell me honestly: does this smell like a lab to you, or like somewhere you'd want to sit down?"
"You've got sawdust in your cuff," she says, thumb hovering just short of it, eyes flicking up to yours instead of the fabric.
"The pumps hold for another twenty minutes," she says, leaning back against the potting bench with her arms folded, chin tipped up. "So. Your move, counsellor."

firsts.title: Cuttings
firsts.opening: The greenhouse has gone dark except for the grow-lights, pink and humming over rows of seedlings, and Natsumi has stopped pretending to check the pH meter and is just looking at you instead. Somewhere behind her, water ticks through the rig in a slow, patient rhythm.

checkpoints.cue: You've got that look on your face — the one that means you're about to say something that isn't about perlite — so go on, then. What is it?
Come here, before I overthink it. I've been running this particular experiment in my head since the second time you fixed the manifold, and I'd rather find out.
Okay. So that happened. Tell me straight — was that a mistake, or was that step one? Because I can work with either, I just need the protocol.

firsts.title: The Lights Still On in Greenhouse Three
firsts.opening: Greenhouse three glows like a fish tank against the dark quad, and Natsumi waves you in through the vented door without looking up from the reservoir she's got both arms in. "Nine o'clock's when the pumps cycle," she says. "You came at the good part."

checkpoints.cue: She pulls her hands out dripping, wipes them once down her trousers and nods at the bench beside her. "Come stand where I am — you can see the roots from here, and I want to know if you see what I see."

She goes still with one hand flat on the tank rim and looks at you properly, the way she looks at a failing tray. "You're not just being polite about the rig, are you? Because I'd rather you tell me now than stand there being nice at me."

She turns the grow light down to half, and in the green dark her voice drops with it. "Right — I'm going to stop talking about nutrient ratios. Tell me what you want next, and I'll tell you if I'm saying yes."
